11400:
Imagine you bake a cake and it turns out absolutely delicious. Now, you have two choices: you can sell the cake while keeping the recipe a secret, OR you can share the recipe with everyone, let them bake it themselves, improve it, add new ingredients, and share their improved version back with the world.

Open-source is the second choice — but for software (computer programs).

When software is open-source, it means:

  1. The underlying recipe — called the source code — is made publicly available for anyone to read.
  2. Anyone is free to use it, study it, modify it, and distribute their own version of it.

That's the heart of it. Everything else is just detail built on top of this core idea.
What Is "Source Code"?

To understand open-source deeply, you first need to understand what source code is, because that's literally the thing being "opened."

Every piece of software — a phone app, a website, a video game, an operating system — is built by humans writing instructions in a programming language. These instructions are called source code. Source code looks like readable text, written in languages like Python, JavaScript, C++, and so on. It's the human-readable "recipe" that tells a computer exactly what to do.

When developers are done writing source code, they run it through a process called compilation or interpretation, which converts it into a form the computer can actually execute — a form that is essentially unreadable gobbledygook to humans. This final, runnable version is often called the binary or executable (think of a .exe file on Windows).

When a company distributes software, they typically only give you the binary — the runnable file. They keep the source code locked away. You can run the software, but you can't see how it was built, you can't learn from it, and you can't change it.

Open-source software is different: the source code is shared alongside (or instead of) the binary, so you get the full recipe.
Open-Source vs. Closed-Source (Proprietary Software)

These are the two major camps in the software world, and understanding the contrast between them makes open-source crystal clear.

Closed-source software (also called proprietary software) is built and owned by a company or individual. The source code is a trade secret. You're allowed to use the software, but only under the company's exact terms — typically after paying for a license. You cannot see how it works, you cannot modify it, and you cannot redistribute it. Think of Microsoft Word, Adobe Photoshop, or macOS. These are polished, powerful tools, but they are black boxes — you use them on the company's terms.

Open-source software, by contrast, hands you the keys. You can look under the hood. You can tinker. You can fix bugs yourself. You can take the code, adapt it for your specific needs, and give it to others. Famous examples include the Linux operating system, the Firefox web browser, the Python programming language, the Android mobile operating system (at its core), the WordPress blogging platform, and the VLC media player.

A useful analogy: think of proprietary software as a car with the hood welded shut — you can drive it, but you can't touch the engine. Open-source software is a car where the hood is always open, the manual is always included, and you're actively encouraged to modify the engine, share your improvements with other drivers, and teach others how to do the same.
A Brief History: Where Did "Open-Source" Come From?

The history here is fascinating and important because it explains why the open-source movement exists at all.

In the very early days of computing (1950s–1970s), sharing software code was completely normal and expected. Computers were so new and so rare that the communities of researchers and engineers who used them freely exchanged code with each other. Software was seen as an academic resource, not a commercial product.

Then, in the late 1970s and 1980s, the personal computer revolution happened. Companies like Microsoft and Apple realized that software could be an enormously profitable product. They began keeping their code secret and selling licenses to use their programs. Software became intellectual property. The welded hood was born.

This commercialization deeply troubled a programmer named Richard Stallman at MIT. In 1983, he launched the GNU Project — an effort to build a completely free, open operating system. In 1985, he founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) and articulated a philosophy: users should have the freedom to run, study, share, and modify software. He called this free software — where "free" meant freedom, not price (a distinction he famously captured as "free as in freedom, not free as in free beer").

Stallman also created one of the most important open-source licenses ever: the GNU General Public License (GPL), which legally enforced these freedoms.

Then in 1991, a young Finnish student named Linus Torvalds wrote the core of a new operating system called Linux and shared it freely with the world. It became one of the most successful open-source projects in history. Today, Linux powers the vast majority of the world's servers, nearly all of Android, and much of the infrastructure of the internet.

By 1998, a group of people — somewhat uncomfortable with the political overtones of "free software" — coined the term "open-source" as a more pragmatic, business-friendly way to describe the same essential idea. The term stuck, and today "open-source" is the dominant term used in the industry.
How Does Open-Source Actually Work? (Licenses)

Just because software is open-source doesn't mean it's a free-for-all with zero rules. Open-source is governed by licenses — legal documents that specify exactly what you can and cannot do with the code.

This is a really important point many beginners miss: open-source doesn't mean the creator gives up all rights. The creator still holds the copyright. The license is how they grant specific permissions to the public. Without a license, no one is actually legally allowed to use, copy, or modify the code, even if the code is publicly visible on the internet.

There are dozens of open-source licenses, but they generally fall into two broad families:

Permissive licenses give you a lot of freedom with very few strings attached. You can use the code, modify it, incorporate it into your own product — even a closed-source commercial product — as long as you give credit to the original author. The MIT License, the Apache License, and the BSD License are the most popular examples. If you've ever seen a small "Licenses" section in a mobile app buried in the settings, the entries there are almost all MIT or Apache-licensed open-source code that the app's developers used as building blocks.

Copyleft licenses are more "viral" or "reciprocal" — they say: you can use and modify this code, but if you distribute your modified version, your version must also be open-source under the same license. The GPL (mentioned earlier) is the most famous example. This is designed to ensure that the open-source ecosystem keeps growing — no one can take open-source code, improve it, and then lock the improvements away behind a proprietary wall.

Choosing between these licenses involves real trade-offs, and developers think carefully about which license fits their goals.
Why Would Anyone Give Away Work for Free?

This is the question most newcomers ask, and it's a great one. The motivation turns out to be surprisingly rich and varied.

Learning and skill-building. Contributing to open-source projects exposes developers to high-quality code written by experienced engineers, gives them practice on real-world systems, and builds a public portfolio of work that future employers can evaluate.

Reputation and career. In the software world, an active open-source profile on platforms like GitHub is often valued more than a résumé. Contributing to a well-known project is a powerful signal of real ability.

Scratching their own itch. Many open-source projects were started because their creator needed a tool that didn't exist, built it, and then shared it. Linus Torvalds needed an operating system for his personal computer. He built Linux for himself and then shared it.

Community and collaboration. There is a genuine, vibrant culture around open-source — a global community of people who enjoy collaborating, debating ideas, and collectively building something greater than any one of them could build alone. Many developers find deep satisfaction in this.

Corporate sponsorship. Many open-source contributors are actually paid to contribute. Large companies like Google, Microsoft, Meta, Red Hat, and Canonical employ engineers specifically to work on open-source projects — because those companies depend on those projects for their own products and infrastructure. Open-source is very much a serious part of the commercial software economy.

Altruism and ideology. Some contributors are genuinely motivated by the belief that software should be a shared human resource, freely available to everyone on earth regardless of wealth or geography — the same way mathematics or language is available to everyone.
The Open-Source Development Process

Open-source projects typically live in a publicly accessible online repository — a structured folder that contains all the code, the history of every change ever made, documentation, and tools for collaboration. The most popular platform for hosting repositories is GitHub (owned by Microsoft), followed by GitLab and Bitbucket.

The typical workflow looks like this: the original creator (the maintainer) publishes the code publicly. Anyone who wants to contribute can make a copy of the code (called forking it), make changes in their copy, and then formally propose those changes to the maintainer (called a pull request). The maintainer reviews the proposed changes, discusses them with the contributor, requests adjustments if needed, and ultimately decides whether to merge the changes into the official codebase.

This distributed, asynchronous, peer-reviewed model of development is one of open-source's great strengths. A project might receive contributions from hundreds of developers across dozens of countries who have never met in person and may never do so.

Bugs are tracked publicly as issues, meaning anyone in the world can report a bug, suggest a feature, or discuss the direction of the project. This radical transparency is fundamentally different from how closed-source software is developed behind closed corporate doors.
Open-Source Is Everywhere — You Use It Daily

This may surprise you: even if you have never intentionally used open-source software, you interact with it constantly.

When you browse any website, the web server delivering that page is almost certainly running on Linux. The web server software itself is likely Apache or Nginx — both open-source. The programming languages used to build the website (Python, PHP, Ruby, Node.js) are open-source. The database storing the information (MySQL, PostgreSQL) is open-source. Your Android phone is built on an open-source Linux kernel. Even the modern internet's foundational protocols — the rules that govern how data travels across networks — were developed in an open, collaborative, publicly documented spirit that closely resembles open-source.

Google's Chrome browser is based on an open-source project called Chromium. The machine learning frameworks that power modern AI tools — TensorFlow (Google), PyTorch (Meta) — are open-source. The programming language Swift (Apple) is open-source. Visual Studio Code, arguably the most popular code editor in the world, is open-source.

Open-source software is the invisible foundation of the modern digital world.
Open-Source Beyond Software

The open-source idea — transparent, collaborative, community-driven creation of shared knowledge — has spread far beyond software.

Open-source hardware applies the concept to physical things: circuit board designs, 3D-printable objects, and electronic components are shared publicly so anyone can manufacture, use, or improve them. The Arduino microcontroller platform is the most famous example.

Open-access science is the movement to make scientific research papers freely available to anyone, rather than locked behind expensive journal subscriptions. Many argue that publicly funded research should be publicly accessible.

Wikipedia is a form of open-source knowledge — an encyclopedia that anyone can read, edit, and improve, governed by community rules rather than a central editorial authority.

OpenStreetMap is the open-source equivalent of Google Maps: a collaboratively built map of the entire world that anyone can use and contribute to.

The Creative Commons licensing system applies open-source-style licenses to creative works like writing, music, photography, and art.

In each of these cases, the same core philosophy applies: transparency, sharing, collaborative improvement, and the idea that freely shared knowledge tends to benefit everyone more than hoarded knowledge does.
Common Misconceptions, Cleared Up

"Open-source means free of charge." Not necessarily. Open-source means the source code is available. A company can charge money for open-source software — for bundling it, supporting it, hosting it, or for the convenience of a polished version. Red Hat is a multi-billion-dollar company built almost entirely on selling enterprise support and services around open-source Linux. What you always get for free from open-source software is the freedom to access and modify the code — but not always a free price tag.

"Open-source software is lower quality than commercial software." This is the opposite of the truth for many of the most critical software systems in the world. The Linux kernel is arguably the most thoroughly tested, battle-hardened piece of software ever written. Open-source software often benefits from thousands of eyes reviewing the code — which tends to surface bugs and security issues faster than a small internal team ever could.

"Publicly visible code means insecure code." The intuitive assumption is that showing everyone your code makes it easier to attack. The security community calls the opposite principle "security through obscurity" — hiding your code and hoping no one figures out the vulnerabilities. Most security experts consider security through obscurity to be a weak strategy. Open-source allows security researchers worldwide to audit the code, find vulnerabilities, and fix them. Many security-critical tools — like the OpenSSL library that encrypts most of the internet's traffic — are open-source.

"Open-source projects are chaotic free-for-alls." Well-run open-source projects have clear governance structures, formal contribution guidelines, maintainers with authority over decisions, and documented roadmaps. Large projects like the Linux kernel have extraordinarily rigorous review processes that are arguably more thorough than many corporate development workflows.

"You can do absolutely anything with open-source code." No — you must comply with the license. If a project uses the GPL, for example, you cannot incorporate it into a closed-source commercial product. Violating an open-source license is a real legal issue and has resulted in actual lawsuits.
The Bigger Picture: Why Open-Source Matters to the World

Open-source represents one of the most significant and successful examples of large-scale human cooperation in modern history. Millions of strangers, motivated by a mix of idealism, self-interest, professionalism, and community spirit, have collectively built the digital infrastructure that underpins the global economy, scientific research, education, and communication.

It has also been a powerful equalizer. A developer in a small town in rural India has access to the exact same high-quality tools — languages, frameworks, operating systems, databases — as an engineer at a Silicon Valley tech giant, for free. This democratization of technology tools is genuinely remarkable.

Open-source has proven that you don't need centralized corporate ownership to produce world-class, reliable, complex software. It has changed how even large corporations think about software development. Today, virtually every major technology company — including Microsoft, Google, Apple, Amazon, and Meta — both uses and contributes to open-source projects, because the collaborative model has proven too powerful to ignore.
Summary

Open-source is a model for creating and distributing software (and increasingly, other creative works) in which the underlying source code — the human-readable recipe — is made publicly available. Anyone can read it, use it, modify it, and share it, subject to the terms of the applicable license. It grew out of a philosophical reaction against the commercialization and secrecy of software in the 1970s–80s. It is governed by licenses, developed collaboratively through platforms like GitHub, and motivated by a mix of altruism, career incentives, corporate sponsorship, and a genuine love of building things together. Today, it forms the invisible foundation of the internet, modern computing, and the digital world you interact with every day.
11401: To understand "operatic," you first need a quick picture of opera itself. Opera is a theatrical art form where a story is performed entirely (or mostly) through singing, accompanied by a grand orchestra, elaborate costumes, and large, dramatic staging. The emotions in opera are never small or quiet. A character doesn't just feel sad — they pour their heartbreak into a soaring, five-minute aria that fills an entire concert hall. A villain doesn't just seem threatening — he booms with a thunderous voice while the orchestra crashes behind him. Everything in opera is turned up to the absolute maximum: the love feels cosmic, the grief feels world-ending, the anger feels explosive. This tendency toward extreme, heightened emotion and grand theatrical scale is the soul of opera — and it is exactly what the word "operatic" is built on.

The adjective "operatic" is used in two related but distinct ways.

1. The Literal Meaning — Directly About Opera

In its simplest, most direct use, "operatic" just means of, relating to, or belonging to opera as an art form. Anything that is a part of, or comes from, the world of opera can be described as operatic.

"She trained as an operatic soprano for fifteen years."

"The composer spent his life writing operatic music."

"It was a grand operatic performance at the famous concert hall."

Here, the word is doing a plain, factual job — it is simply telling you that the thing being described belongs to the world of opera. There is no hidden meaning, no judgment, no exaggeration implied. A soprano who sings opera is an operatic soprano. A score written for an opera is an operatic score. Simple.

2. The Figurative Meaning — Dramatic, Exaggerated, Over-the-Top

This is the meaning you will encounter far more often in everyday writing, conversation, and media. When "operatic" is used figuratively, it means something is excessively dramatic, wildly theatrical, extravagant in emotion, or larger-than-life in style — just like opera itself.

In real life, when a person or situation is described as "operatic," it means the emotions or behavior involved are blown way out of proportion, or carried out with a grand, theatrical flair that goes well beyond what feels ordinary or restrained. The intensity, the scale, the flamboyance — it all feels like something lifted straight from an opera stage.

"When her flight got cancelled, she had an operatic meltdown at the airport counter — weeping, gesturing dramatically, and declaring it the worst day of her life."

"The couple's relationship was intensely operatic — passionate declarations of love one week, explosive arguments the next."

"The film's finale was operatic in its scale, with sweeping music, crumbling cities, and characters delivering grand speeches."

In all of these examples, "operatic" is pointing to something that is heightened, intense, and emotionally large — something that feels more theatrical and excessive than calm, measured reality normally is.
The Emotional Flavor: Is It a Compliment or a Criticism?

This is an important nuance, because "operatic" can go either way depending on context — and understanding this is what separates a good learner from a great one.

When used as praise or admiration: "Operatic" can express awe at something that is genuinely grand, sweeping, and emotionally powerful in a beautiful way. When a film, a piece of music, a speech, or a piece of writing is called "operatic," it can mean it achieves a rare kind of emotional magnitude — it moves you deeply, it feels epic, it reaches for the sublime.

"The novel ends with an operatic final chapter that left readers in tears."

"Beethoven's symphonies have an operatic intensity that few composers have ever matched."

Here, the word carries a sense of breathless admiration. The scale and drama are seen as strengths — as signs of artistic ambition and emotional power.

When used as gentle mockery or mild criticism: "Operatic" can also suggest that someone is being unnecessarily over-dramatic about something that doesn't deserve such a reaction. It implies an element of excess, self-indulgence, or theatrics that are out of proportion with reality. The person is, in a sense, performing their emotions rather than simply feeling them.

"He gave an operatic sigh and collapsed onto the sofa when asked to take out the trash."

"Her apology was so operatic — lots of tears and gasping — that nobody quite believed it was sincere."

Here, the drama is being gently laughed at. The word quietly says: this is a bit much, don't you think?

The key is this: when the drama is earned and moving, "operatic" is a compliment. When the drama is excessive or unwarranted, "operatic" is a polite eyebrow-raise.
The Core Idea to Lock In

"Operatic" always points to one central quality: extreme, heightened, larger-than-life intensity — emotional, theatrical, or dramatic in a way that feels grand and excessive, like something from an opera.

Whether the word is used literally (about actual opera) or figuratively (about real life, films, writing, or behavior), it is always gesturing toward something that refuses to be small, quiet, or understated. The scale is big. The feelings are enormous. The style is theatrical. Nothing is half-hearted. Everything is turned to the maximum.
A Quick Guide to Using It Yourself

You can safely use "operatic" when describing:

Behavior or reactions: A person whose emotional responses are dramatically over-the-top. ("His operatic fury over a parking ticket bewildered everyone.")

Relationships: Love stories or conflicts that are passionate, intense, and volatile in a grand way. ("Their operatic romance ended as dramatically as it began.")

Art, film, music, literature: Works that are emotionally sweeping, grand in scale, and intensely dramatic. ("The director's style is unapologetically operatic.")

Events or situations: Real-world events that unfold with dramatic intensity, high stakes, and theatrical twists. ("The trial became an operatic spectacle watched by the entire country.")

The beauty of this word is that it carries the whole world of opera inside it — the grandeur, the excess, the emotional intensity, and the theatrical scale — and drops all of it onto whatever it is describing. Whenever you see or hear it, ask yourself: is this drama earned and magnificent, or is it a bit too much? Context will always tell you which way it leans.
11402: Operation refers to the act of something being done, carried out, or made to work. It can describe a machine functioning, a procedure being performed, an organized effort toward a goal, or a mathematical action on numbers. The central idea running through all its uses is: deliberate action taking place — something actively happening.

When a machine, system, or service is doing what it's supposed to do, you say it is "in operation."

  • "The water pump has been in operation since 1995." — It has been running and doing its job since 1995.
  • "The escalator is not in operation today." — It is not working today.

Here, "operation" simply describes the state of something actively functioning.

Common phrases in this meaning:

  • In operation — currently working: "The new bridge is now in operation."
  • Come into operation — to begin being used: "The new traffic rules come into operation next week."
  • Put into operation — to start using something: "They put the new system into operation immediately."
  • Out of operation — not working: "The machine has been out of operation for days."
2. A Planned, Organized Activity Toward a Goal

This is one of the richest and most common uses. An operation can be any coordinated effort — involving steps, people, and a clear purpose — aimed at achieving a specific result. The key idea is that it is not random; it is planned and purposeful.

  • A rescue operation — a coordinated effort to save people in danger
  • A search operation — an organized effort to find someone or something
  • A military operation — a planned military action (attack, retreat, mission, etc.)
  • A relief operation — an organized effort to provide help after a disaster
  • A sting operation — a secret plan by police to catch criminals in the act
  • A covert operation — a secret, hidden operation, often by intelligence agencies

Military operations are sometimes given proper names: Operation Overlord was the Allied invasion of Normandy in World War II. The word "Operation" before a name signals an organized, named military or official mission.

The scale can vary enormously — from a small two-person operation to a massive international effort involving thousands of people.

In medicine, an operation (also called a surgical operation) is a procedure in which a surgeon physically works on a patient's body — cutting, repairing, removing, or correcting something — to treat a medical condition.

  • "She had an operation on her spine."
  • "The operation to remove the tumour lasted four hours."
  • "He's recovering well after the operation."

In informal British English, people often shorten it to "op": "He had an op last Thursday."

In mathematics, an operation is a specific, defined action you perform on one or more numbers to produce a result. The four basic mathematical operations are:

  • Addition (+): combining numbers → 5 + 3 = 8
  • Subtraction (−): removing one number from another → 9 − 4 = 5
  • Multiplication (×): scaling a number → 6 × 7 = 42
  • Division (÷): splitting a number into equal parts → 20 ÷ 4 = 5

Beyond these basics, more advanced maths introduces further operations: squaring a number, finding a root, taking a logarithm, etc.

The word "operation" fits here because you are doing something to the numbers — performing an action that transforms them.

When people talk about the operations of a company, hospital, school, or government body, they mean the practical, day-to-day activities that keep it running. This covers all the processes, systems, and tasks involved in making the organization function smoothly.

  • "She manages operations at a logistics company." — She oversees the practical running of the business.
  • "The day-to-day operations of the hospital are complex."
  • "Our operations team ensures products are delivered on time."

This is why many organizations have an Operations Manager or a Head of Operations — someone responsible for making sure the machinery of the organization (not literally, but figuratively) runs without problems.
6. The Way Something Works or Takes Effect (Abstract Use)

"Operation" can also refer to the way in which a principle, force, law, or mechanism works and produces effects — even when no physical action is being done.

  • "The operation of gravity keeps the planets in orbit." — The way gravity works and functions.
  • "The operation of this law is complex." — The way this law actually works and takes effect in practice.

This meaning is slightly more formal and abstract. It essentially treats something (a law, a force, a rule) as if it were a machine doing its job, and describes how it functions.

• Operation (singular) usually points to a specific, single event: "a rescue operation," "an operation on her knee," "Operation Desert Storm."
  • Operations (plural) usually points to ongoing, collective activities: "business operations," "military operations," "the operations department."
Summary of All Meanings at a Glance

ContextWhat "operation" means
Machine/systemThe act of it running and functioning
Organized effortA planned, purposeful activity toward a specific goal
MedicalA surgical procedure performed on a patient
MathematicsAn action performed on numbers (add, subtract, etc.)
BusinessThe day-to-day activities that keep an organization running
AbstractThe way a force, rule, or mechanism works and produces effects
The Single Thread That Ties Everything Together

No matter the context, "operation" always carries the sense of something actively happening in a controlled or deliberate way — a system doing its job, a plan being carried out, a procedure being performed, or an action transforming something into a result.

Think of it as the doing word in noun form — not just an idea, but an idea in action.
11403: The adjective operative revolves around one central concept: something that is active, working, and actually having an effect in the real world. Think of it as the opposite of something that exists only on paper, or has stopped working, or hasn't kicked in yet. When something is operative, it is live — it is doing its job right now.
Meaning 1: Currently Active and In Effect

This is the most general use of operative. When a law, rule, plan, system, or mechanism is described as operative, it means it is currently functioning, in force, and producing real effects.

The new traffic rules become operative from next Monday.

This means: starting next Monday, those rules are no longer just written words — they are in force. They have real power. You must follow them.

The safety regulations are operative throughout the construction site.

Here, it means those safety rules are not suspended, not paused, not theoretical — they are actively applied right now at that location.

A very natural opposite to remember is "inoperative" — meaning broken, no longer working, or no longer in effect.

The elevator is currently inoperative.

(It exists, but it is not functioning.)

So operative and inoperative work like a switch: something is either on (operative) or off (inoperative).
Meaning 2: "The Operative Word" — The Most Important Word

This is perhaps the most famous and widely used form of this adjective, and it is worth understanding deeply because you will encounter it constantly in English — in books, conversations, journalism, and everyday speech.

When someone says "the operative word is X," they mean: X is the single most crucial, most meaningful word in what was just said — the one word that changes everything, carries a hidden condition, reveals the real point, or defines the true meaning.

Think of it like spotlighting one word in a sentence and saying: this is the word you must pay attention to. This is what actually matters.

Example 1:

"He said he would try to attend the meeting." — "Yes, and the operative word there is 'try.'"

What the speaker is pointing out: The word try is the key. It doesn't mean he'll definitely come. The word try is doing all the work — it carries a warning that his attendance is uncertain. If you miss the word try and assume he's coming for certain, you've missed the point entirely.

Example 2:

"She agreed to review the proposal." — "The operative word is 'review' — she hasn't agreed to approve it."

Here, review is doing all the heavy lifting. Someone might celebrate that she agreed to look at it, but the operative word reminds you: looking at something is not the same as accepting it.

Example 3:

"The discount is available for a limited time." — "The operative word is 'limited' — don't wait too long."

The word limited is what matters. Everything else in the sentence is secondary.

In every case, the operative word is the word that, once you notice it, shifts your entire understanding of the statement. It's often where a condition, a catch, a nuance, or the real meaning is hiding.

You can also say "the operative phrase" when it's a group of words doing this job, rather than just one word.

In medicine, operative is used as an adjective to describe anything connected to a surgical operation.

  • Pre-operative — before the surgery (pre means "before")
  • Post-operative — after the surgery (post means "after")
  • Operative procedure — the surgical procedure itself
  • Operative risk — the risk involved in performing surgery
  • Operative site — the area of the body where surgery is being performed
  • Operative care — care given during or in connection with a surgery

The patient's post-operative recovery was smooth.
The doctor discussed the operative risks before proceeding.

Here, operative simply acts as a label that connects something to the context of surgery. It doesn't mean "working" in this case — it means "of or relating to an operation (surgery)."
Meaning 4: The One That Is Actually Producing an Effect

In a more formal or literary register, operative can describe the particular factor, element, or force that is actually causing something to happen or playing the deciding role among several possible candidates.

Among all the factors that led to her success, the most operative was her discipline.

This means: discipline wasn't just one factor among many equal ones — it was the one actively driving her success. It was the most powerful force at work.

Fear of failure was the operative emotion guiding his decisions.

Here, operative points to fear as the emotion that was truly in the driver's seat, actively shaping his choices.

This usage is closely related to Meaning 1 — it still carries the sense of "actively working and producing an effect," but now applied to identifying which specific element is most alive and powerful within a situation.

Once you see the central idea — actively working, in effect, having real power — all the meanings make sense as variations of the same theme:

  • A rule that is operative is one that has real, active power (not dormant).
  • The operative word is the one doing the real work in a sentence (not decoration).
  • Operative procedures are actions that directly involve working on the body through surgery.
  • The operative factor is the one actually making things happen (not passive or irrelevant).

The thread tying everything together: operative always points to what is genuinely active, effective, and doing the real work — whether that is a law, a word, a surgical act, or a force in life.

If you want to test whether operative fits a sentence, ask yourself: Is this thing currently active? Is it producing real effects? Is it the one that truly matters here? If yes, operative is likely the right word.
11404: Operose is an adjective with two closely related meanings, depending on whether you use it to describe a task or a person.
Meaning 1 — Describing a Task or Activity

When used to describe a task, project, or piece of work, operose means something that is tediously laborious — demanding a great deal of effort, time, and painstaking care, often to an almost exhausting or burdensome degree.

Think of it as sitting somewhere between difficult and tiresome. An operose task is not just hard — it is grindingly demanding, the kind of work that drains you slowly because it requires sustained, meticulous effort over a long stretch of time.

Examples:

  • Copying out an entire encyclopedia by hand is an operose undertaking.
  • Sorting thousands of handwritten historical records one by one is operose work.
  • Writing a single paragraph that requires you to cross-check fifty sources before every sentence is an operose exercise.

Notice the common thread: the work is extensive, painstaking, and wearisome — not just challenging in a sharp, sudden way, but grinding in a slow, heavy way.

When used to describe a person, operose means industrious — someone who works hard, diligently, and with great effort.

This meaning is essentially the human embodiment of the first meaning. Just as operose work demands extraordinary effort, an operose person is one who puts in extraordinary effort.

Example:

  • She was an operose scholar who spent decades compiling her research.

In this sense, the word is closer in feel to diligent or assiduous, and it carries a tone of quiet admiration.

Here is something crucial that separates operose from simple synonyms like hard or difficult:

Operose almost always carries a tone of tedium or wearisomeness. It subtly signals that the effort involved is not exciting or thrilling — it is grinding. When you call something operose, you are not celebrating how impressively challenging it is. You are acknowledging how exhaustingly laborious it is.

This is why, when describing a person as operose, the word can sometimes feel slightly double-edged — it acknowledges their hard work, but also hints that what they do is the kind of slow, painstaking, unglamorous toil that most people would find draining.
How Operose Differs from Similar Words

• Laborious — very close in meaning, but operose adds a stronger sense of tedium and wearisomeness.
  • Arduous — means physically or mentally demanding and tough, but doesn't carry the same slow, grinding, tedious quality. Climbing a mountain is arduous. Manually indexing ten thousand documents is operose.
  • Diligent / Industrious — when used for people, these are cleaner synonyms, but operose is rarer, more formal, and sounds more literary.
  • Tedious — captures the boring, drawn-out quality, but misses the element of effort. Operose things are both effortful and tedious at the same time.
When Would You Actually Use It?

Operose is a formal, literary, and somewhat rare word. You are more likely to encounter it in older texts, academic writing, or formal prose than in everyday conversation. Using it in casual speech would sound unusual or even affected. But it is a genuinely useful word in formal writing when you want to convey, with a single precise adjective, that something is both heavily demanding and wearily tedious — a combination that no common everyday word quite captures as efficiently.

Operose describes either a task that demands grinding, painstaking, and wearisome effort, or a person who works with that same kind of tireless, diligent industry — and in both cases, the word carries an undercurrent of toil rather than triumph.
11405:
An opiate is a drug that comes directly from opium — a thick, milky substance found naturally inside the seed pods of a plant called the opium poppy. Think of opium as the raw source material, and opiates as the specific drugs extracted or processed from it.

The most well-known natural opiates are morphine, codeine, and thebaine. Heroin is also derived from morphine, making it a close relative, though it is semi-synthetic (chemically modified in a lab from a natural opiate).

The opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) produces seed pods. When these pods are cut, a white sap oozes out. When that sap dries, it becomes raw opium — a sticky brown substance. Scientists then isolate and refine specific chemical compounds from this raw opium to create individual opiates like morphine and codeine.
What opiates do to the body

Your brain and nervous system naturally have special "docking stations" called opioid receptors. Your body actually produces its own natural chemicals (called endorphins) that attach to these receptors to reduce pain and create feelings of calm and well-being — like the natural "high" you might feel after exercise.

Opiates work by mimicking those natural chemicals. When you take an opiate, it attaches to those same receptors in your brain and spinal cord, and produces several powerful effects:

Pain relief: Opiates are extraordinarily effective at blocking pain signals before they fully register in the brain. This is their most important medical use.

Euphoria: Opiates trigger a strong sense of pleasure, warmth, and well-being — sometimes described as a wave of intense relaxation and happiness.

Sedation: They slow down the brain and nervous system, making the person feel drowsy and calm.

Slowed breathing: This is the most dangerous effect. At high doses, opiates suppress the brain's drive to breathe, which is the main cause of opiate overdose deaths.

In medicine, opiates are some of the most powerful pain-relieving drugs available. Morphine is widely used in hospitals to manage severe pain — after major surgery, serious injuries, or in cancer patients. Codeine is milder and is found in some prescription cough medicines and lower-strength painkillers. They are also used to treat severe diarrhea, since opiates slow the movement of the intestines.
The serious danger: addiction and dependence

Opiates are among the most addictive substances known. Two things happen with repeated use:

Tolerance develops first — your body gets used to the drug, so you need a larger and larger dose to feel the same effect.

Physical dependence follows — your body adjusts its chemistry around the presence of the drug. When you stop taking it, you experience painful withdrawal symptoms: sweating, chills, nausea, intense muscle aches, and severe anxiety. This physical pull makes it extremely hard to stop.

Beyond physical dependence, opiates also create psychological addiction — a powerful mental craving and compulsion to keep using the drug, even when the person knows it is harming them. This combination of physical and psychological dependency makes opiate addiction one of the most difficult to treat. The global "opioid crisis" — a major public health emergency — is largely rooted in the overprescription of opiate-derived drugs and the resulting wave of addiction and overdose deaths.
Opiate vs. Opioid — an important distinction

These two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, but they have distinct technical meanings.

Opiates are drugs derived directly and naturally from the opium poppy — morphine, codeine, thebaine.

Opioids is the broader umbrella term that covers three categories: natural opiates, semi-synthetic drugs made by chemically modifying natural opiates (like heroin or oxycodone), and fully synthetic drugs designed in a laboratory to act on the same brain receptors (like fentanyl or methadone).

So all opiates are opioids, but not all opioids are opiates. In casual speech and even in much journalism, "opiate" and "opioid" are used loosely to mean the same thing — but in a medical or scientific context, the distinction matters.

The word "opiate" is also used figuratively — outside of medicine — to describe anything that numbs people's awareness, dulls their critical thinking, or keeps them passive and content without addressing real problems. The most famous example is Karl Marx's phrase: "Religion is the opiate of the masses," meaning he saw religion as something that made people accept suffering rather than challenge the systems causing it. You might hear people use "opiate" in this way to describe entertainment, social media, or propaganda — anything that soothes people into passive acceptance.

"After the surgery, the doctor administered a small dose of an opiate to keep the patient's pain under control."

"Morphine is a powerful opiate that has been used in medicine for over two centuries."

"The government launched a campaign to reduce dependence on opiates after a sharp rise in overdose deaths."
11406:
To opine means to express or state your personal opinion on something — to openly declare what you think or believe about a subject.

It simply means to give your view. When someone opines, they are not reporting a fact. They are sharing what they personally think is true, right, or best. The opinion belongs to them, and they are putting it out into the world.
But There's More to It Than That

If "opine" just meant "to say what you think," we'd have no need for it — we already have words like think, believe, say, and feel. What makes "opine" special is the flavor it adds.

When you say someone opined, you are subtly hinting that they stated their view with a certain confidence and weight — as if they felt their opinion was worth declaring, even if nobody asked for it. There's often a quiet suggestion that the person is being a little self-important, pompous, or overly certain about a view that is, after all, just their personal take.

Think of it this way: thinking something happens inside your head. Saying something is neutral. But opining is a slightly theatrical, self-assured act of putting your view forward, often in formal or elevated language, sometimes with an air of authority.
The Tone: Formal with a Hint of Irony

"Opine" belongs to formal or literary language. You won't hear it much in casual conversation. You'll find it in newspapers, legal writing, formal essays, and books.

And here's the interesting part — writers often use it with a gentle touch of irony or sarcasm. When a journalist writes "the commentator opined that the film was a masterpiece," there's often a subtle, barely-hidden smirk in that sentence. The writer is suggesting that this is merely one person's grand proclamation, not a universal truth.

So the word can be used both seriously and with dry humor, depending on context.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Think / believe — These describe what is happening inside your mind. You can think something privately and tell no one. Opining is always an outward act — you are expressing it.

Say — Completely neutral. You can say anything — a fact, a question, a joke. Opining specifically involves personal viewpoint.

Claim / assert — These suggest you are presenting something as though it were a fact. Opining is softer — it signals clearly that this is personal opinion.

Suggest — This is tentative and gentle. Opining is more confident and declaratory.

So "opine" lives in a specific lane: it is outward, opinion-based, confident, and slightly formal — all at once.

The most common structure is: opine that + [your view]

  • The professor opined that modern architecture had lost its soul.
  • The elderly senator opined that young people no longer respected tradition.
  • She opined that the new policy would do more harm than good.

You can also opine on or about something:

  • He happily opined on everything from food to foreign policy.
  • The critic opined about the novel's weak ending for twenty minutes.

You can also opine without any following clause, simply as a way to describe someone who is in the act of giving their views:

  • "She opined freely whenever given a microphone."

Imagine a retired judge sitting at a dinner party. Nobody asked him, but he leans forward, clears his throat, and declares: "This city's leadership has completely failed its citizens." He says it with full confidence, as if delivering a verdict.

A journalist writing about this dinner would not say he mentioned or whispered that. They would say he opined it — because it was a bold, self-assured expression of personal view, delivered with a certain air of authority. And depending on the journalist's tone, that single word choice could either respect the judge or quietly poke fun at his pompousness.

That is the full life of the word opine — to express a personal opinion, often with confidence, often in formal settings, and often carrying just a faint whiff of someone who is a little too pleased with their own views.
11407:
If someone is opinionated, it means they hold strong opinions about things — and they hold onto them firmly. They don't just have views quietly in their head; they express those views confidently, often without being asked, and they're not easily persuaded to change their mind, even when challenged with solid arguments.

Think of it this way: everyone has opinions. But not everyone is opinionated. What sets an opinionated person apart is a combination of three things working together:

  1. Strong conviction — they don't sit on the fence. They believe their view is clearly right.
  2. Free expression — they voice their views readily, sometimes without waiting for an invitation to do so.
  3. Resistance to change — they hold their position stubbornly, even when others push back.

Remove any one of these, and the person is just "someone with opinions." Put all three together, and you have someone opinionated.
Is It a Positive or Negative Word?

When used to describe a person, "opinionated" almost always carries a slightly negative or critical tone. It's not a harsh insult, but it's not really a compliment either. It suggests that the person's confidence tips over into stubbornness, and that they may not genuinely listen to other points of view.

Compare these:

  • "She's confident." → clearly positive
  • "She's opinionated." → slightly critical — implies she's firm to the point of being closed-minded

That said, how negative it sounds depends on the context. In casual conversation, "he's pretty opinionated" might simply mean "he knows what he thinks and isn't shy about it" — said with mild amusement rather than harsh judgment. But the word never fully loses that edge.
Why "Opinionated" Is Different from Just "Having Opinions"

This is the most important distinction to understand.

A person can have strong political beliefs but still genuinely listen to the other side, change their mind when presented with evidence, and engage in calm debate. That person is not really opinionated in the true sense of the word.

An opinionated person, on the other hand, tends to:

  • Share their views without being asked — you didn't invite the topic, but here they are
  • Present their opinion as though it were fact, or as the only sensible position to hold
  • Make the conversation feel one-directional — they're not really curious about your view, they're asserting theirs
  • Be difficult to reason with, because in their mind, the matter is already settled

In short: having opinions is universal; being opinionated is a personality tendency characterized by assertiveness and inflexibility combined.

• "My grandfather is very opinionated about politics — once he's decided something, no argument will change his mind."
  • "She gave such opinionated feedback that it left no room for any other ideas."
  • "He's too opinionated to work well in a team; he never really considers anyone else's suggestions."
  • "I asked her what she thought of the restaurant, but she was so opinionated that it turned into a ten-minute lecture."

In each case, you can feel the slight edge. There's a sense that this person goes beyond simply having views — they impose them, or at least are very reluctant to let them go.

"Opinionated" works well with modifiers:

  • "Slightly opinionated" — has clear, firm views but can still have a real conversation
  • "Very opinionated" — strong views + clear resistance to changing them
  • "Incredibly/outrageously opinionated" — the person essentially steamrolls others in conversation
When Can It Be Used Positively?

Occasionally, "opinionated" is used in a neutral or even admiring way, especially in contexts where decisiveness and strong direction are valued:

  • "We needed an opinionated leader who would make bold calls without endless debate."
  • "She's an opinionated designer — she won't let a project go out the door unless it meets her standards."

Even here, though, there's a subtle undercurrent of "this person is strong-willed and not always easy to deal with." The word very rarely becomes purely flattering. If you want to compliment someone for having conviction, words like decisive, principled, or assertive do a cleaner job.
A Special, Very Common Usage: In Technology

In the world of software and technology, "opinionated" has a specific, widely-used meaning that is neutral or positive.

An opinionated tool, framework, or system is one that has already made strong design decisions for you. It tells you: this is how you will structure things, this is the way things are named, this is the workflow you'll follow. It doesn't leave those choices up to you.

The opposite is called unopinionated (or "flexible") — a tool that gives you freedom to make all those decisions yourself.

Example: "Ruby on Rails is an opinionated web framework — it enforces a specific way of organizing your project."

This is positive in context because an opinionated tool can save enormous time and debate. You don't have to agonize over decisions the tool has already made well.

The connection to the human meaning is clear: just as an opinionated person has already decided what the right way is and won't deviate, an opinionated tool has already decided the "right way" to do things — and it holds firm to it.

Understanding how "opinionated" sits next to related words sharpens the meaning significantly:

Assertive — Being assertive simply means expressing yourself clearly and confidently. It's a positive quality. "Opinionated" goes further, adding the element of stubbornness and the implication that the person isn't truly open to being wrong.

Stubborn — "Stubborn" focuses primarily on the refusal to change, regardless of the topic. "Opinionated" focuses on the having and asserting of strong views. They overlap, but stubbornness is about resistance; being opinionated is about the views themselves combined with resistance.

Outspoken — An outspoken person speaks their mind freely and boldly, but this is often seen as a positive trait — like speaking truth to power, or being honest when others stay silent. "Opinionated" is more about excessive confidence in one's own views, not just willingness to voice them.

Dogmatic — This is a stronger, more formal word. A dogmatic person treats their beliefs as absolutely certain and beyond question — often in the context of ideology, religion, or rigid systems of thought. "Opinionated" is the everyday, lighter version of this.

Headstrong — Headstrong emphasizes acting on your own judgment even when others advise you differently. It's about action as much as views. "Opinionated" is more about expressing and defending views.

Someone opinionated is a person who holds strong, firm views on many things, expresses them freely and assertively, and is resistant to changing them — a trait usually seen as a mild character flaw, suggesting self-assured close-mindedness rather than healthy confidence.
11408:
An opponent is a person (or a group) who is against you in a contest, competition, argument, debate, or any situation where two sides are clearly divided.

Think of it this way: whenever there is a structured clash — a game, an election, a debate — the person or team on the other side is your opponent. And importantly, the relationship is mutual: if you are my opponent, then I am also yours.

1. In a contest or competition

This is the most common use. In sports, games, elections, legal proceedings, or debates, your opponent is whoever you are directly competing or contending against.

  • A boxer and the person he is fighting in the ring — they are each other's opponents.
  • Two chess players sitting across a board — each is the other's opponent.
  • Two candidates running for the same political position — each is the other's political opponent.
  • Two teams playing a football match — each team is the other's opponent.

2. Against an idea, policy, or plan

"Opponent" also refers to a person who is publicly against something — not necessarily competing against another person, but opposing a concept, proposal, or course of action.

  • "She is a strong opponent of the death penalty." (She is firmly against it.)
  • "The opponents of the new highway project organized a protest."

In this use, the opponent isn't in a game or a race — they simply stand in opposition to something.

Neutrality. This is perhaps the most important quality of the word. An opponent is not necessarily your enemy. The word describes a structural relationship — you are on opposite sides in a specific context — but it carries no automatic suggestion of hatred, hostility, or ill will. You can deeply respect your opponent. A tennis player may admire the skill of her opponent even while trying to beat her.

A defined context. The opponent relationship exists within a specific situation. Once the game ends, or the debate concludes, the opponent relationship may simply dissolve. Two people who were opponents in a chess tournament can be perfectly friendly strangers afterward.

Directness. An opponent is specifically and directly against you (or your side). This is different from, say, a competitor in a market, who may not even be targeting you personally.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Understanding what makes "opponent" different from nearby words helps you use it precisely.

Opponent vs. Enemy
An enemy implies hatred, hostility, and a desire to cause harm. The word carries emotional weight. An opponent is far more neutral. You face an opponent; you despise an enemy. A rival tennis player is your opponent — calling them your "enemy" would sound extreme and personal.

Opponent vs. Rival
A rival suggests an ongoing, repeated competition — often with a personal or emotional edge, sometimes involving jealousy or ambition. Rivals compete repeatedly over time and are deeply aware of each other. Opponents may face each other just once. Two companies that have competed for decades are rivals; the team you play against this Sunday is your opponent.

Opponent vs. Competitor
A competitor is someone pursuing the same goal or prize as you, but the word doesn't necessarily mean you are directly facing each other. In a race with twenty runners, all nineteen others are your competitors, but the person running directly beside you and matching your pace stride-for-stride might be called your opponent in the heat of the moment. "Competitor" is also very common in business contexts (other companies selling similar products), while "opponent" feels more natural in structured contests.

Opponent vs. Adversary
An adversary is more formal and serious. It suggests a sustained, significant opposition — often in high-stakes situations like politics, law, or war. All adversaries could loosely be called opponents, but not all opponents are adversaries. You wouldn't normally call your chess partner your "adversary."

• "Before the match, the coach told us to study our opponent's weaknesses."
  • "My debate opponent made several strong points, and I had to think quickly to respond."
  • "The senator's opponents voted against every bill she introduced."
  • "He treated his opponent with respect, shaking hands both before and after the game."
  • "She is a well-known opponent of online censorship and has written books on the subject."
  • "Our opponents in the final round are the defending champions — this will not be easy."
  • "The lawyer prepared carefully, knowing her opponent in court was highly experienced."
Common Collocations (Words That Often Appear with "Opponent")

These are word combinations you will encounter frequently:

  • Formidable opponent — a very strong, difficult-to-beat opponent
  • Worthy opponent — an opponent who deserves respect because of their skill or strength
  • Political opponent — someone opposing you in the political arena
  • Face your opponent — to confront or go up against them
  • Defeat/beat your opponent — to win against them
  • Underestimate your opponent — to think your opponent is weaker than they actually are (usually a mistake)

When referring to more than one, you simply say opponents.

  • "Our opponents played brilliantly tonight."
  • "She has always treated her opponents fairly."

An opponent is anyone who is on the opposing side from you in a contest, game, election, debate, or structured conflict — or anyone who formally stands against an idea or policy you support. The word is neutral in tone: it describes a position (opposite to yours) without implying hatred. It is tied to a specific context and often temporary. It sits in a family of similar words — rival, enemy, adversary, competitor — but is the most balanced and broadly usable among them.
11409:
"Opportune" describes something that happens or is done at exactly the right time — a time that is perfectly suited to a purpose, a need, or a situation. When something is opportune, the timing is so well-matched to the circumstances that it makes things easier, more effective, or more likely to succeed.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that it is fundamentally about timing. Something isn't opportune just because it's good — it's opportune because it's good at this particular moment, and that moment makes all the difference.
Breaking it down with a simple image

Imagine you've been trying to ask your boss for a raise, but you've been waiting for the right moment. One day, your boss walks in extremely happy because the company just landed a huge contract. You think: "Now is the time." That moment — right then, when your boss is in high spirits and the company is doing well — is an opportune moment. The timing lines up perfectly with your goal. If you had asked the week before, when the company was struggling, the timing would have been wrong. But now, it's just right.

That feeling of "just right timing" is the heart of opportune.
What can be described as opportune?

The word is most naturally attached to time-related nouns. You will most often hear or read:

"An opportune moment" — the most common pairing. It refers to a specific point in time that is ideal for doing something.

"An opportune time" — slightly broader than a moment, but same idea. A period or point when conditions are favorable.

"An opportune occasion" — a particular event or situation that happens to be well-suited to doing something.

You can also describe an arrival, a discovery, a silence, or an interruption as opportune if the timing of that thing is what makes it valuable. For example, a rainstorm can be opportune for a farmer whose fields are dry. A phone call can be opportune if it comes exactly when you needed advice. The common thread is always: the timing fits the need.
The key nuance — it's not just "good," it's "good right now"

This is the sharpest edge of the word, and it's worth pausing on. "Opportune" is not a synonym for simply "good," "helpful," or "useful." A warm coat is useful, but you wouldn't call it opportune unless it appeared at the exact moment you were freezing. Opportune always implies that the timing of something is what gives it its value.

Think of it this way: the same action, the same event, or the same word can be opportune in one moment and completely useless — or even harmful — in another. Offering someone a joke might be opportune when they're stressed and need lightening up, but deeply inopportune at a funeral. The word is asking you to pay attention to when, not just what.

The opposite of opportune is inopportune, which means happening at a bad or wrong time. An inopportune moment is one where the timing works against you. If your phone rings loudly during a job interview, that is an inopportune interruption. If you bring up a sensitive topic right when someone is already upset, that is an inopportune time to do so. Understanding this opposite locks in the meaning of opportune even more firmly: it lives entirely in the world of timing.

Opportune is a positive word. It suggests that the timing is genuinely good — not just acceptable, but notably well-suited to the situation. When you call a moment "opportune," you're saying that if you had to design circumstances to make this action or event most effective, you'd have chosen this moment. It carries a sense of fortune or luck aligning with purpose.

You can intensify it — "a most opportune moment," "a perfectly opportune time" — to emphasize just how ideal the timing is. But even on its own, the word already leans strongly positive.
How opportune differs from similar words

Several words are close to opportune but not identical.

Timely is the nearest relative. Something timely arrives or happens before it's too late — it beats a deadline or prevents a problem. Opportune is slightly richer: it doesn't just mean "not too late," it means the timing is actively, specifically favorable. A timely warning stops danger; an opportune warning does so at the ideal moment when it can do the most good.

Well-timed is nearly identical to opportune and can often be swapped for it. Opportune is simply the more formal and literary of the two.

Convenient means easy or suitable for someone's needs, but it lacks the sense of a specific moment aligning with circumstances. Convenient is about ease; opportune is about timing.

Favorable describes conditions being good, but doesn't pin it to a specific moment in time the way opportune does.

None of these words are wrong to know alongside opportune, but the thing that makes opportune itself is always that precise, well-matched, well-timed quality.
One important word to not confuse it with

Do not confuse opportune with opportunistic. They share a root, but they are very different in meaning and tone.

Opportune is neutral-to-positive and simply means well-timed. Opportunistic, on the other hand, describes a person or behavior that selfishly takes advantage of a situation — often in a calculating or unprincipled way. Calling someone "opportunistic" is usually a criticism. Calling a moment "opportune" is simply a description of good timing. They are not interchangeable.

Opportune is a moderately formal word. You'll encounter it in books, articles, speeches, and careful writing. In very casual conversation, people are more likely to say "good timing" or "the right moment," but opportune fits naturally in professional, academic, and literary contexts. It never sounds out of place in writing.
Putting it all together — examples in context

"She arrived at an opportune moment — the meeting had just started and nothing important had been said yet."
Here, her timing was ideal because she didn't miss anything.

"He waited patiently for an opportune time to raise the issue with his manager."
He was looking for a moment when conditions — the manager's mood, the workload, the atmosphere — would make his request most likely to succeed.

"The discovery of water was opportune for the hikers, who had nearly run out of supplies."
The discovery happened exactly when it was most needed, which is what makes it opportune rather than just fortunate.

"This is not the most opportune moment to bring that up."
A gentle way of saying the timing is wrong — the circumstances right now are not well-suited to whatever is being suggested.

In summary: something is opportune when its timing is just right — when the moment aligns so well with a need, a goal, or a situation that things are made easier, more effective, or more successful as a direct result. The word lives entirely in the realm of timing, and its quiet power comes from how precisely it captures that feeling of "this is exactly the right moment."
